extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent practitioners, and USPTO examiners handling appeals to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB)
extracted.subtask_short: PTAB appeal procedure and oral hearing
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive rules for prosecuting appeals to the Board (filing fees, timing, jurisdiction, remands, oral hearing requests, examiner participation, and Board decisions). Guidance is aimed at appellants and examiners on how to proceed before and after the Board exercises jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal forwarding fee – timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellant must pay the appeal forwarding fee set forth in § 37 CFR 41.20(b)(4) within the later of two months from the date of either the examiner's answer, or a decision refusing to grant a petition under § 1.181 to designate a new ground of rejection in an examiner's answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensions under § 1.136(a) are not applicable; see § 1.136(b) (patent applications) and § 1.550(c) (ex parte reexamination) for available extension mechanisms. The examiner's answer should notify the appellant of the fee and deadline. It is preferable to pay the forwarding fee when filing any reply brief. Effective March 19, 2013, the appeal brief fee was reduced to $0 and a forwarding fee was added; waiver rules apply for those who paid before that date. The forwarding fee does not apply to inter partes reexamination appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to pay appeal forwarding fee – consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the appeal forwarding fee is not paid within the required period, the appeal will stand dismissed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appeal is dismissed by rule; the examiner should proceed as indicated in MPEP § 1215 regardless of whether a separate paper is mailed dismissing the appeal. Waiver of the requirement may apply for appellants who paid the earlier appeal brief fee before March 19, 2013.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for oral hearing – when and how to file
rubrics_metrics.description: An oral hearing should be requested only when appellant considers it necessary or desirable. To request a hearing, file a separate paper captioned 'REQUEST FOR ORAL HEARING' accompanied by the fee set forth in § 41.20(b)(3) within two months from the date of the examiner's answer or on the date of filing of a reply brief, whichever is earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form PTO/SB/32 may be used. If the written request is not filed in a separate paper with the required caption, or is not timely filed or accompanied by the fee, the request is improper and the appeal will be decided on the briefs without an oral hearing. Extensions of time are only available via § 1.136(b) (or § 1.550(c) for ex parte reexamination). An appeal decided on the briefs receives the same consideration as one decided after an oral hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board may deny an oral hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding submission of a proper request for oral hearing, the Board may decide that a hearing is not necessary and will notify appellant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples when Board may deny a hearing include situations where the Board is convinced the examiner's position cannot be sustained or where the Director orders a remand. The Board's discretion under § 41.47(f) means filing a request does not guarantee a hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral hearing time limits and order of argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral argument is ordinarily limited to twenty minutes for appellant and fifteen minutes for the primary examiner unless otherwise ordered. Appellant will argue first and may reserve time for rebuttal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If appellant needs additional time, file a separate request well in advance to the Clerk of the Board; granting extra time is within the panel's discretion. Any unused appellant time may be used for rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and argument permissible at oral hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: At the oral hearing, appellant may only rely on evidence previously entered and considered by the primary examiner and present argument relied upon in the brief or reply brief, except as permitted for new arguments based on recent relevant Board or Federal Court decisions upon a showing of good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary examiner likewise may rely only on argument and evidence relied upon in the examiner’s answer, except that upon a showing of good cause the primary examiner may present a new argument based on a recent relevant decision. See form paragraph 12.279.03 for examiner request to present oral arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing scheduling, confirmation, waiver, and no refund
rubrics_metrics.description: A notice of hearing stating date, time, and docket is sent to appellant. If appellant fails to confirm or waives the hearing, the appeal will be removed from the hearing docket and decided on the briefs. No refund of the hearing request fee will be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If appellant confirms but then does not appear, the appeal will be decided on the briefs. Appellant should inform the Board as early as possible of changes to avoid wasting Board resources. Petitions to vacate a decision or related scheduling requests have narrow allowances (see other guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Special hearing accommodations and technical requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellant may request special hearing arrangements (particular date/time, telephone/audio‑video argument, use of projector) by filing a separate paper addressed to the Clerk of the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telephone/audio‑video requestor bears the cost and must ensure software compatibility; the Board's IT specialist may contact appellant. Projector use is subject to availability; appellant must provide their own laptop or mobile device for presentations (e.g., PowerPoint®). Requests will be considered so long as they do not unduly delay the case or impose administrative burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescheduling hearings – discouraged and requires convincing reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Rescheduling a hearing is discouraged and will not be granted in the absence of convincing reasons that do not unduly delay issuance of any patent based on the application or place undue administrative burden on the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such requests should be made in writing in a separate paper addressed to the Clerk of the Board and made well in advance. The Board considers administrative burden and delay when evaluating rescheduling requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner participation in oral hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: If the primary examiner wishes to appear and present oral argument, the examiner must request the opportunity on a separate letter using form PTOL-90 and form paragraph 12.279.03.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the examiner participates, the examiner is typically given 15 minutes to reply and present a statement setting forth the examiner's position. The examiner may normally rely on arguments and evidence in the examiner’s answer; new arguments based on recent decisions are allowed upon showing good cause. Examiners associated with the appeal should notify the usher on the day of the hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public attendance and decorum at hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the public may attend oral hearings in appeals of reexamination proceedings, reissues, and published applications; members of the public are not permitted at appeals of non-published applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those attending should follow Hearing Room Protocol/Decorum; appropriate attire is clothing suitable for an important business meeting. More info available at the USPTO public hearing info page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction over the appeal – beginning and end
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdiction passes to the Board upon filing of a reply brief under § 41.41 or upon expiration of the time to file such a reply brief, whichever is earlier. Jurisdiction ends upon (1) remand by Director/Board, (2) Board final decision, (3) express abandonment complying with § 1.138, (4) filing an RCE under § 1.114, (5) appellant failure to take required action leading to dismissal, or (6) appellant reopening prosecution under § 41.40(b) or in response to a new ground of rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents (like IDS or petitions) filed while the Board has jurisdiction are typically held in abeyance until jurisdiction ends except for petitions authorized by the part. If the Board determines the file is incomplete or noncompliant, it may relinquish jurisdiction to the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board or Director remand – authority and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the Director and the Board may remand a case to the examiner when necessary; remand transfers jurisdiction back to the examiner and, under § 41.50(e), a remand by the Board is not appealable (not final for judicial review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On remand, the examiner should take action consistent with the remand order; absent specific guidance, the examiner should take an action described in MPEP § 1207. Director-ordered remands may be used where there is a change in the law requiring a new ground of rejection (e.g., to prepare a substitute examiner’s answer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute examiner's answer after remand – appellant options and deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: If a substitute examiner's answer is written in response to a remand for further consideration of a rejection (37 CFR 41.50(a)(1)), the appellant must within TWO MONTHS from the date of the substitute examiner's answer either (A) reopen prosecution before the examiner or (B) maintain the appeal by filing a reply brief under 37 CFR 41.41.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reopening prosecution requires filing a reply under 37 CFR 1.111 with or without amendment, affidavit, or other evidence relevant to the remand; such a request is treated as withdrawing the appeal. A reply brief accompanied by amendment/affidavit/evidence will be treated as a request to reopen prosecution. Failure to timely select an option results in sua sponte dismissal of the appeal as to the claims subject to the remand. Extensions under § 1.136(a) do not apply to the TWO MONTH period; see § 1.136(b)/§ 1.550(c) for extension options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval/signature requirements for substitute examiner's answer and reopening
rubrics_metrics.description: A Technology Center (TC) Director or designee must approve every substitute examiner's answer by signing; supervisory patent examiner approval is required for actions withdrawing a final rejection and reopening prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph guidance instructs insertion of TC Director's signature and reasons supporting rejections in the substitute examiner's answer. Supervisory approvals per MPEP §§ 706.07(e) and 1002.02(d) are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board consideration of amendments filed during jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board is not obligated to consider new or amended claims filed while it has jurisdiction over the appeal; however, certain proposed amendments (e.g., canceling claims without affecting scope of others or rewriting dependent claims into independent form) may be remanded for examiner consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 1206 for when remand for amendment is appropriate. The Board can refuse to consider claim changes made during its jurisdiction except in limited circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand to consider affidavits or declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations filed with the notice of appeal but before jurisdiction passes to the Board will be considered for entry only if appellant makes the necessary showing under 37 CFR 1.116(e) as to why they are necessary and were not earlier presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits/declarations filed after final rejection and prior to notice of appeal are handled by other MPEP sections. If evidence was not treated by the examiner, the Board or Director may remand to permit examiner consideration. Generally, Board does not remand affidavits submitted in connection with a rehearing where no rejection was made under 37 CFR 41.50(b); such affidavits, if not remanded, are considered only as arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand by Board for further search – rarity and required search depth
rubrics_metrics.description: It should be extremely rare for the Board to remand a case to the examiner for further search; if remand is necessary, the Board should conduct a search (online or otherwise) of at least one subclass and cite art from that subclass to demonstrate the basis for concluding a further search would be material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A remand for further search extends pendency and may necessitate patent term adjustment under 35 U.S.C. 154(b). The art cited by the Board need not be art upon which a rejection can be made; it should demonstrate that searching the area would be material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board may require additional briefing under § 41.50(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may order appellant to additionally brief any matter that it considers of assistance in reaching a reasoned decision on the pending appeal; appellant is given a time period to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include applicability of particular case law or prior art not previously identified. Consideration of IDS filed while Board has jurisdiction is held in abeyance. Failure to timely comply with such an order may result in sua sponte dismissal of the appeal. Extensions of time are available only under § 1.136(b). The decision to make a requirement under § 41.50(d) is discretionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board decision outcomes – affirmance, reversal, remand, and new grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may affirm or reverse the examiner's decision in whole or in part on the grounds specified by the examiner, may remand the application to the examiner, and may include a new ground of rejection in its opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmance of rejection on any specified grounds constitutes general affirmance for that claim except as to any specifically reversed ground. A new ground of rejection is designated as such and is not final for judicial review; appellant has two months to either reopen prosecution (amend/submit new evidence) or request rehearing under § 41.52 addressing the new ground with particularity. Remands included in Board decisions are not final for judicial review; after remand proceedings conclude the Board may adopt its earlier decision as final or render a new decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: New ground of rejection by Board – appellant's response options
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Board designates a new ground of rejection, the appellant must within two months either (1) reopen prosecution by submitting appropriate amendments or new evidence to have the matter reconsidered by the examiner (leading to remand), or (2) request rehearing under § 41.52 addressing the new ground and stating with particularity the points believed to have been misapprehended or overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new ground is binding on the examiner unless an amendment or new evidence not previously of record in the examiner's opinion overcomes it. Failure to timely file a request for rehearing waives any arguments that the decision contains an undesignated new ground of rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition to withhold decision to permit refiling
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellant may petition that the decision be withheld to permit refiling of the application at any time prior to mailing of the decision; up to 30 days may be granted although the Board generally limits the time as much as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board is more likely to grant an early-filed petition that obviates the necessity for an oral hearing or the setting of a hearing date. If the case has been set for oral hearing, the petition should include a request to vacate the hearing date. A withdrawal of the appeal filed on the same day that the decision is mailed will lead to denial of a petition to vacate the decision.
